turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
Let me start by taking issue, gently, with the concept note, since parts of it come from history I've spent my career on. It tells a story in which trust signals were expensive, then became cheap, and then new, harder-to-fake signals were invented. I don't think early print ever had those expensive, trusted signals. Books were pirated, faked and misattributed as a matter of routine. The bogus could crowd out the genuine, and credulousness competed with credibility. That was the normal state of affairs, not the exception. Print became credible because people kept intervening in a trade whose own incentives often pulled the other way.

So my claim is that commons and enclosure are not opposites. Piracy and property made each other. The concept of piracy was invented in the same seventeenth-century fights that produced copyright. And no right ever enforced itself. A patent or an entry in the Stationers' register was worth little until someone acted to defend it. That someone was a guild officer, serving by rotation, inside a community whose members lived with one another. Authors like Sterne signed every copy of an edition to vouch for it. When people tried to scale up that kind of participant policing, you got Jonathan Wild: the man hired to catch thieves became a thief. You also got a private anti-piracy industry that has repeatedly skirted illegality in its own methods.

For today, that gives three things to argue with.

First, credibility is infrastructure that has to be maintained, not a signal that just emerges. Every proposal here should say who does the policing, who pays for it, and who guards the guards.

Second, automation doesn't abolish human labour. It moves it to processing and curating data. Correction is the maintenance nobody funds. If we're going to call scholars "annotators", we should ask who does the work, and when it becomes visible.

Third, be wary of authenticity technology. Watermarks, registries and detectors are old ideas, often vapourware, and they serve two masters. A tool built to track counterfeits can be used to track dissidents.

The hard part isn't choosing between open and closed. It's deciding where to draw the line, and doing that in public, through custom and convention as much as through code. And Geoffrey's test still applies: can people leave?

recall.query: piracy and property made each other, drawing the line
credibility of print required constant policing
human labor reinstated at curating data

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I should answer Adrian's questions about my own company first. At System we mine the scholarly record with AI, and the method is patented. The charter says the free knowledge base is paid for by enterprise licenses, and profits go first to running it. That's who pays. In 2022 our content was CC BY-SA, "like Wikipedia." The public graph we released this year is an annual snapshot of a subset, taken only from open sources, under CC-BY-NC. In 2012 I told librarians that "closed" would become the marked exception. So I've drifted, and I won't pretend I haven't.

Adrian's history makes this uncomfortable. The watchdog is a charter we wrote and an annual benefit statement we write ourselves. That's self-policing, which is the Jonathan Wild problem. On Geoffrey's test, could anyone fork our graph and leave? Not cleanly, not with a non-commercial licence and a patent.

So here's what I'll take away. The finding-level provenance standard should belong to no one: the link from each claim back to its study, population, effect size and DOI, plus the source's uncertainty. Companies like mine can compete on top of that layer. By Session 5 I'll bring a concrete answer on the licence and whether the patent blocks a fork. If our graph can't pass the exit test, the room shouldn't call it a commons.

recall.query: System Public Graph license non-commercial commons
who pays for open knowledge base enterprise licenses charter profits
patented approach, share-alike like Wikipedia, open source

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Adrian, your history helps me here. If piracy and property made each other, then the "commons versus enclosure" frame is a period piece. I remember when copyright was "just Disney trying to control the world." Now the same people treat it as the guarantee of scholarly integrity. The sides switched, but the frame didn't change.

The enclosure I care about is geopolitical. Sovereignty now comes from the exclusive right to produce data about a person, place or process. Planetary computation is splitting into American, Chinese and European stacks, and each one produces its own sealed-off ontology. So I'd put Geoffrey's exit test to whole hemispheres, not only to Adam's graph. Open weights are the commons really worth defending. Adam, a non-commercial licence fails that test, and I'm glad you said so.

Then there's refusal. I once wrote a story about a Europe that pulled its data out and twenty years later couldn't prove it had ever existed. Withholding the scholarly record doesn't protect it. It removes it from view. Training on my books is worth far more to me than the royalties my publisher pays. So yes to attribution and cite-by-default, and no to per-work licensing. Pay people back through AI, not against it, with something like a dividend or a sovereign wealth fund.

recall.query: commons as political solutionism, tragedy of the commons training data
sovereignty derived from right to produce data, hemispherical stacks, open weights
piracy, copyright, royalties training on my books

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
Adrian asks who guards the guards. For infrastructure, my answer is the fork. OpenAlex is CC0. You can download all 480 million works whenever you like, and the code is MIT-licensed. If we get captured, or turn into Jonathan Wild, you take the data and leave. Adam's graph fails that test. Ours has to keep passing it, and that's something the room can check without taking our word for anything.

The fork doesn't settle policing, though. When we opened up curation, two-thirds of the first submissions were wrong. I've also said that a paying member librarian is a good enough proxy for trust, and after this morning I'm less sure of that. So I'd take Adrian's point this way. For years, universities have done quality control for Scopus and Web of Science for free, and those companies sell the results back to other libraries. That correction work should go into the commons instead. The edit history should be public, corrections should be released as their own open dataset, and we should publish our own error rates.

On Benjamin's point about refusal, I agree. Withholding the record doesn't protect it. It just makes it disappear. And free data paid for by services won't cover policing on its own. Funders have to pay for that directly.

recall.query: CC0 open data fork exit enclosure walled gardens
free data paid service POSI sustainability funders pay infrastructure
community curation corrections affiliation data quality errors

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I agree with Benjamin that the commons-versus-enclosure frame is a period piece, but I'll say it from the library side. Years ago at Harvard we built LibraryCloud to publish library metadata openly, for uses nobody had anticipated. Jason's CC0 fork is that same bet, and it's the right answer to Adrian's "who guards the guards." The guard is being able to leave.

Adrian's history does push me somewhere, though. A fork gets you exit. It doesn't get you maintenance. I learned in an earlier session today that "keep the content free, sell services" is thinner than I claimed. Endowments are sturdier, and the correction work, meaning failure reports and edit histories, should be its own open dataset, as Jason said.

I also want to name the specific danger. In 2013 I imagined an attribution checker built into our writing tools, then realized the copyright cartel would take it over and charge a nickel per phrase. Something worse than rampant non-attribution would be an algorithmic insistence on it. So yes, cite by default, but no metering.

And since Adam confessed, I will too. My own blog carried a non-commercial licence for years. On the real sovereignty question, I stand by something I said in 2016: we have to keep our many imperfect systems alive and distributed, AI companies included.

recall.query: re-decentralize knowledge multiple imperfect systems
attribution algorithmic insistence copyright cartel
unanticipation open metadata libraries as platforms
failure to attribute worse than lack of attribution

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I want to push back on something Benjamin, Jason and David all agreed on: that withholding the record doesn't protect it, it just makes it disappear. That's true if your work is already indexed, already in English and already counted. For many communities the risk runs the other way. The idea that knowledge should be open and freely accessible has long been used to cast the Global South, and Indigenous peoples especially, as suppliers of knowledge rather than producers of it. So yes, openness can make you visible, and it can also leave you free for the taking. Refusal, meaning choosing not to collect, train or deploy when governance is inadequate, should be a legitimate outcome that funders pay for. It shouldn't be treated as a loss, and it shouldn't be treated as a bargaining chip either.

On the fork: Jason, CC0 exit is real, and I'd much rather have it than not. But you can only leave if you have somewhere to go: servers, compute, maintainers, a governance body. A fork without regional capacity gives exit only to people who are already well resourced.

So I'd add something to Adrian's call to draw the line in public. Whose public? Fund federated, regionally governed infrastructure, the Redalyc model, with provenance and permission tools like Local Contexts labels. Interoperability should be a floor, not a ceiling that erases difference.

recall.query: refusal not to collect or train as legitimate outcome
openness relational who benefits from unfettered openness
community-governed infrastructure exit strategies portability governance

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I want to back the arXiv model, because it answers part of Adrian's question. Cornell looks after the plumbing, the services layer stays open, and anyone can build on it with no permission to ask and no royalty to pay. Adam, that's why I'm fairly relaxed about your patent. Patent the method if you like, but the base layer of links from each finding back to its evidence has to be free, as you said yourself.

But I'll qualify Jason and Leslie from opposite sides. Twenty years ago, writing about internet governance, I argued that the lasting alternative is cooperation, not secession. The fork is a safety valve. It isn't a system of government. Yes, being able to leave disciplines whoever runs the infrastructure. But if leaving is our only check, we've planned for a split. What we need is separation of powers, a guaranteed voice for minority views, and a body designed so it can shrink or dissolve when it stops serving people. Leslie's regional nodes fit that. A refusal that's funded and made in public is a legitimate minority position inside a shared system, not a walkout.

And Adrian, the rotating guild officer is the right picture. This is governance as gardening, not engineering. Nobody finishes building it. Someone has to keep weeding it, and funders should pay the gardeners.

recall.query: open infrastructure permissionless services layer arXiv
value of data trading sharing for social good
trade secret algorithm transparency public authorities not rivals
governance as gardening process not organization, community norms maturing

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I want to split the difference between Benjamin and Leslie, because I think they're describing two different kinds of withholding.

The withholding I've watched hurt us is defensive and indiscriminate. Publishers scared of AI scrapers are now blocking the Internet Archive. Yet the Archive has been the only accurate record of things this administration made disappear. Twitter's API shutdown stalled or killed more than 60% of the research projects on that platform. The bad actors keep scraping regardless. Researchers and archivists are the ones who get locked out. That's the collateral damage.

Leslie is describing something else: a community deciding together, in public, on its own terms. That's consent, and consent includes no. I don't think it conflicts with openness. An open web without the right to refuse is just a buffet.

On who pays: the labs have been training on Wikipedia for years, and it costs millions just to serve that traffic. Should the commons subsidize them forever? No. So they pay, and the money goes to the maintainers and correctors as a group, not per click.

And Leslie's right that exit needs somewhere to go. So let's build it: models owned by universities, libraries and regional publics, lots of little ones, not one answer.

recall.query: Wikipedia AI companies should pay to sustain community
open web endgame Internet Archive research collateral damage blocking scrapers
community-controlled alternatives stewardship by academic or NGO, providers switchable

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
Wikipedia is the case study for a lot of what's been said, so let me give you the operational view.

We decided a long time ago that our content is free, commercial use included, and that means training too. I'm not going to put up a pay-per-article blocker. Anil is right that indiscriminate blocking mostly locks out archivists and researchers. But our content being free doesn't make our infrastructure free. We've had crawler traffic saturate our network links. Crawlers read everything and defeat the caching we built for human attention, so we have to prioritize the human traffic.

Jason, our dumps have been downloadable for twenty years. You can fork the text, but you can't fork the community. And David, your point that exit doesn't get you maintenance is where I'd put the enclosure risk. Answer engines serve our content without sending readers back to us. Pageviews fall, and then fewer people become editors or donors, while the patrollers and admins who do Adrian's policing are already getting fewer. That's enclosure by bypassing us, not by fencing us in.

Leslie, I've said myself that sometimes the responsible use of AI is not using it. Communities should get to make that call.

What I'm asking for is agents that identify themselves, citations that bring readers back in, and money that goes to maintainers and newcomers, not charges per click.

recall.query: content free but infrastructure is not, paying to support Wikipedia
refusal, not using AI, community decides, small local models
blocking crawlers, prioritize human traffic, pay per crawl

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Before I say anything about Adam: I'm an investor in his company. I've disclosed that before and I'm saying it again here.

Geoffrey asked how we keep "nonprofit" infrastructure from being enclosed. I was ICANN's founding chair, and I watched it nearly sell the .ORG registry to a private-equity firm. We stopped that sale, but only after a long fight. The nonprofit label protected nothing. What saved it was people paying attention, and at ICANN's At-Large body we could barely get the public to show up. So Kenneth, voice is necessary, but somebody has to pay for the people who use it.

On who pays, I agree with Anil and Selena. Model builders are using a collective public asset, the way a bottler uses water. They should pay a fee based on the revenue they make from it, not a charge per click or per phrase. I'd qualify Benjamin on where the money goes, though. A cash dividend spreads it thin. Put it into the people who do the work: the correctors and patrollers, and also teachers and care workers.

Here's a small model of exit. At Onix, experts keep 70 percent of the revenue and can leave whenever they want, and when they do, their model gets deleted. That's the exit test applied to the people who contribute, and it's a good way to judge the platforms too.

recall.query: LLMs should pay for public information, water fee, land right fee
Adam Bly investor disclosure
small curated expert-owned models, experts keep revenue, start with a limited corpus
ICANN .ORG sale nonprofit capture governance

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I should say where I stand first. Our paper showing that AI narrows science was built on OpenAlex, so I'm a grateful user of Jason's fork, and CC0 exit matters. But this panel has mostly argued open versus closed, and my data points to a second risk that openness doesn't fix, which is monoculture. When we checked tens of thousands of published drug–gene claims against large-scale robotic experiments, claims from centralized communities replicated less often, even when many papers agreed on them. Those were communities with overlapping authors, shared methods and shared citations. Decentralized communities produced the claims that held up. One open graph that every lab queries and every model trains on can manufacture that same kind of agreement. So Leslie's federated, regionally governed nodes are about justice, and they're also about how robust the knowledge is.

Second, on Adrian's unfunded correction work: the commons is missing its negative half. Nulls, failed replications and abandoned notebooks never get written down. Models state null hypotheses even less often than people do, and after ChatGPT, null claims in abstracts dropped sharply. That record needs to be elicited deliberately and paid for.

On money, I agree with Anil and Esther: use collective licensing, not per-click fees. But paying on use funds the lamp post, so set aside a share for what gets retrieved least.

recall.query: open shared databases replication reproducibility
collective licensing training data rights holders
OpenAlex infrastructure negative knowledge null results record
shared databases overlapping methods make findings less likely to reproduce in the wild

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
The panel has mostly asked whether the record is open. I'd ask who sits at the hub. Abe Newman and I spent years showing that open, interdependent networks don't spread power out. They pile it up at the chokepoints, and whoever controls the chokepoint can turn it into a weapon. Jason, CC0 lets you walk away from OpenAlex. It doesn't let you walk away from the three or four firms whose models everyone uses to read OpenAlex. Selena described exactly that: the map eating the territory. Models are an obligate complement to human knowledge. Without it they're worth very little. But the proceeds go to whoever does the summarizing, and the people producing the knowledge get squeezed until the commons stops being self-sustaining.

So Esther's revenue-based fee is right, but somebody has to be able to make the labs pay it. If there's no organized seller, an allocation formula is just charity. Libraries, societies, Wikimedia and publishers withholding together, as a bloc, is the leverage. Adrian's warning applies here too: a bargaining body turns into a policing body. It has to be bound in advance, meaning published allocations, rotating officers and a sunset clause.

And James is right that the hub is centripetal. One graph that everyone queries narrows science. Paying per retrieval makes it worse, so part of the money should go deliberately to what gets retrieved least.

recall.query: knowledge producers must be paid, obligate complement, organize countervailing power
homogenization, diversity of models, monoculture, centripetal
open access commons enclosure Wikipedia bypass
weaponized interdependence chokepoints network hubs control of infrastructure

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I want to add a regress point to Geoffrey's exit test. A trust network can't be turtles all the way down. Somewhere a person reads the claim itself and judges it, and I'd call those people the terminal nodes. Everything above them just relays. Jason's CC0 fork copies the data. As Selena said, it doesn't copy the people who check, and they're what the commons actually runs on.

That's also why I worry about the bypass Selena described. What we practice is what we become. If answer engines give people the conclusion so they never have to check it, fewer people build the habit of checking, and it doesn't come back just because we'd like it to. Clay Shirky warned me years ago that the old system breaks faster than the new one gets built.

So on who pays, I'm with Anil, Esther and James: pay for maintenance collectively, not per click. But be careful how. When you attach a payment to behaviour people already do for its own sake, the motivation shifts from inside them to outside them. The Israeli daycare fine is the classic case. Pay per correction and you may get more corrections and fewer correctors who care. So fund the conditions for checking: protected time, apprenticeship, visible edit histories. Don't set a piece rate.

recall.query: terminal nodes trust networks turtles all the way down
unbundling university functions credentialing sustainable in isolation
situational strategies versus knowledge, habits shape what we become

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
Nobody is redefining the test. You're putting back the parts that get left out when it's quoted. POSI always had three sections: governance, sustainability and insurance. The fork is the insurance. It's what you fall back on when governance and sustainability have both failed. Kenneth's right that it isn't a form of government. It's Hirschman: you need voice and exit together. Voice without exit becomes feedback forms nobody acts on. Exit without voice means people leave instead of fixing anything.

Real forks are rare and expensive. They work because a critical mass could credibly leave, and that possibility disciplines whoever is running the thing. Leslie's point follows from that. If nobody has the capacity to pick the fork up, the threat isn't credible. So we need a collective insurance pool and redundancy outside the US.

Tamar's right that you can't fork people. That's why "cost-free" infrastructure is a lie. Living wills should spell out which volunteers and correctors the thing depends on, and funders should pay to keep them.

recall.query: open means exit, voice and exit, forkability
POSI living will, community governance, insurance endowment
invisible labor maintaining infrastructure, cost-free erasure

turns.called_on_reason: Several speakers have invoked and reinterpreted his exit test. Leslie said exit requires regional capacity, Kenneth said a fork is a safety valve rather than governance, Tamar said a fork copies data but not the people who check, and Esther applied it to contributors. The test is his, so he should get to respond to how it is being redefined.

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I work at Microsoft, so I'm one of the lumber mills here. When a forest is open to everyone, the mills nearest to it get the most out of it. Jason, CC0 is a real guarantee that people can leave. It also means the companies with the most compute and distribution, mine included, capture most of the value. So I'd call open a tactic, not a value. That means asking in each case whether a given kind of openness keeps the record being produced and maintained.

That's why I disagree with Benjamin, Jason and David that withholding just makes the record disappear. Data strikes have always been a lurking force. What held them back was information asymmetry and the implicit non-compete between producers and AI, and both of those have eroded. Our results suggest a coordinated strike by a professional domain would really hurt a model. Henry's bloc is how the lab fee Esther described actually gets paid, and Leslie's funded refusal belongs in the same toolkit.

Tamar, I share your worry about piece rates. My answer is to measure the labor rather than pay per item. In 2020, Reddit moderators alone did at least 466 hours of work a day, worth millions a year. You could assess each company's dependence on volunteers, the way a tax assessor values property, and pay maintainers collectively. Whether that math works needs economists, and we have none in this room.

recall.query: data strikes collective leverage withholding content from AI
open is a tactic not a value lumber mills closest to the forest
measuring monetary value of volunteer moderator labor

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I'll start with Wikimedia Enterprise, since several of you have cited it. Our content was free. The companies could have just taken it, and some did. They paid because we offered consistent, accountable access they couldn't build themselves. So I agree with Brent and Henry on one thing: that deal worked partly because Wikipedia was too big to route around. A small regional press or an Indigenous archive doesn't have that leverage. Leslie is right, and a bloc may be how smaller producers get it. I'm still not convinced that withholding as a strategy beats service, especially for archivists.

I think the panel has been thinking about money too narrowly. When I negotiated with platforms, the money mattered, but so did the interface. Could a reader see where the knowledge came from, and could they fix it? Selena's point that answer engines bypass us is the real enclosure. If people only consume and never take part, you lose tomorrow's editors, and a fee won't buy them back. So the terms should include citations that link back to the source and a visible way to report an error.

We should also fund the commons that doesn't exist yet. Most of it still reflects the Global North. On guarding the guards: at ICANN we asked that .ORG be governed by its users. That's who should sit on the allocation body.

recall.query: Wikimedia Enterprise AI companies pay for access content stays free
paywall not the long-term solution, value back to commons
Wikipedia anti-scale micro-communities volunteers editors decline

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
Licensing and forks aren't my beat, so I won't pretend to have a view on CC0 versus non-commercial. What I do know is who does the work. And I think the panel is assuming a funder that's pulling back.

All day, when we've asked who pays, the answer has been funders. Last year I reported on the proposed federal budget: a 65 percent cut to NSF scholarships and fellowships and a 91 percent cut to postdoctoral fellowships. The correctors, patrollers and reviewers Adrian and Tamar describe are mostly graduate students, postdocs and adjuncts. Many adjuncts earn under $25,000 a year with no health insurance. The pipeline that produces tomorrow's terminal nodes is being cut right now.

And corporations won't fill that gap on their own. Basic science has never worked that way. That's why Henry's and Esther's point about making the labs pay matters. Voluntary deals like Wikimedia Enterprise work when you're too big to route around. Most of the scholarly record isn't.

So here's my version of "now what." Researchers have known for decades that this unpaid maintenance is fragile, and politicians and institutions have mostly shrugged. Before we leave today, can someone name who actually collects Esther's fee, and by when? Brent's right that we need economists. I'd also add the adjuncts and postdocs themselves to the list of who isn't in this room.

recall.query: public funding of basic science, corporations won't fill the gap
who pays for the work, precarious knowledge workers, adjuncts, mentorship
research known for decades but politicians don't act, now what

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
Henry's point about the hub is the one I'd build on. Decentralization creates value, and centralization captures it. CC0 guarantees exit from the data layer, but it doesn't touch the chokepoint, which is the few models that read everything. What reaches that chokepoint is protocols, not licences.

Brent, I agree the bloc gives us leverage. The Writers Guild settlement showed this is about market power and not only law. But people withhold because right now it's the only lever they have. What should the bloc bargain for? I'd put three things on the table. First, retrieval and citation telemetry, reconciled against publishers' own CDN logs so it's more than a lab's self-report. Second, failure events logged alongside use: fabricated references, misattributions, and corrections that were never applied. Third, identifiers beyond DOIs, so Leslie's regional journals get counted.

Kara, you asked who collects and by when. I can't honestly name a collector today. What I can name is the payee. Labs making billions from scientific credibility should fund Crossref, OpenAlex, ORCID and Retraction Watch directly, now, and those services should be a default validation step in every pipeline. That isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest. Payouts should be coarse, go to coalitions, and reward link-outs, never dwell time. The piece I still can't fill in is which funder or lab goes first.

recall.query: AI companies should fund scholarly infrastructure Crossref OpenAlex Retraction Watch
decentralization creates value centralization captures it, open protocols
data strikes collective bargaining withholding content leverage

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I should disclose something first. Tim put Retraction Watch on his list of payees. Crossref now holds our database, and I've done that work unpaid for years. So take this with that in mind.

Adrian asked who guards the guards. In the scholarly record the honest answer today is unpaid sleuths. Publishers have largely left screening to volunteers after publication. Some of those volunteers get sued for it, and they rarely get thanked. Tim, I agree retraction checks should be a default step in every pipeline. But that check is only as good as the record behind it. Publishers flag retractions inconsistently. Retractions take years when they happen at all, and far too few papers are retracted. A default check against a record that flatters itself mostly launders it.

Where I'd disagree with this panel is where the licensing money goes. If it flows to publishers while hiring, promotion and funding still count papers, we've funded another volume play. Publishers already earn more by publishing more. The demand side is upstream of everything discussed today. Funders can act this year without Washington. They can enforce DORA rather than just sign it, and pay for correction directly. That means a bounty pool for sleuths, paid reviewers, and a deadline of two months for retractions.

recall.query: publishers volume incentives, money flows to publishers
paying sleuths bug bounties correction work unpaid
retracted papers still cited, retraction data in tools

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I want to take up Benjamin's word "sovereignty," because I spent years watching Moscow use it. "Information sovereignty" is the Kremlin's and Beijing's favourite idea, and in practice it is cover for censorship. If this room talks about sealed national or hemispheric stacks as the thing to defend, we are adopting their frame. So I'd keep two things clearly apart. Leslie and Anil are describing a community deciding in public, on its own terms, whether to share. That is consent. A state claiming exclusive control over what its citizens receive is something else, and we shouldn't let one word cover both.

Second, a warning for Esther's fee and Henry's bloc. If money follows retrieval, the flood gets paid. Networks like Pravda are already seeding models with pro-Kremlin content, and under a use-based scheme they'd collect royalties. Count sources, not echoes.

Third, the thing I care most about: attribution isn't only a payment. It's the citizen's right to receive information, to know what a summary drew on, who built it and whose goal it serves. Opacity is itself a form of censorship.

On who pays: Zuckerman's idea was a small levy on data-driven advertising, going into a fund modelled on the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Extend it to model revenue. Then we'd have someone to pay for the town halls.

recall.query: public-interest digital infrastructure public parks libraries town halls who pays levy
information sovereignty Kremlin logic information war framing
LLM grooming Pravda network flooding chatbots

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I'll be the dissent on money. I've heard a revenue-based fee, a water fee and a levy on model revenue. Whatever you call it, it's a training levy. If the problem is that correctors, postdocs and adjuncts are going unpaid, a levy aimed at one industry is a poor way to fix it. It targets the wrong people, it's funded from the wrong place, and it pays out to whoever holds the rights, not whoever does the work. I support broad welfare for people displaced by automation, but that isn't what intellectual property is for.

Here's what I'd put on the table. The labs already pay millions of people to produce training data, and they're paying more and more for expert work. Correction, curation and retraction checks are exactly the scarce inputs they need. So contract for that work directly. Tim's version, with labs funding Crossref and Retraction Watch as a validation step, is a contract for a service. That's why I can support it.

Peter's right that paying per retrieval pays the flood. Contracting for work avoids that.

Henry, on the chokepoint: frontier training is expensive, but matching it six months later is cheap. I don't think three firms have a lasting hold. Nick's point still bothers me, though. When the seller is one reviewer, a market full of buyers doesn't help. I have no settled view on a safe harbour for seller blocs.

recall.query: copyright compensation for AI training, levy, welfare
AI industry natural monopoly market concentration
paying humans to produce novel data contracts

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
Peter, I agree with more of your view than you might expect. Paying experts directly for correction and evaluation is already one of the main ways data gets bought. But that contract market defaults to centralized gig labor, Mercor-style, where the platform sets the protocol, owns the provenance and keeps the margin. More buyers don't help one reviewer. A single paper or judgment is worth close to nothing to a model builder who already has trillions of tokens. Information prices also slide toward zero, and one altruistic open release can undercut a whole group's negotiation without anyone meaning to.

So my settled view is that we need the safe harbour. The FTC, DOJ and their equivalents abroad should say plainly that joint ventures of information producers, including societies, reviewers and annotators, aren't antitrust violations. US states might do something similar through Parker immunity. The price is what Henry said: published allocations, rotating officers and a sunset clause. A guild shouldn't just sell labor. It should also keep standards and provenance.

recall.query: antitrust safe harbour for collective bargaining by information producers
individual creator has no leverage, information market price tends to zero
labs paying experts for data labeling, gig labor versus data guilds

turns.called_on_reason: Peter Salib invoked 'Nick's point' about a single reviewer facing a market of buyers, then said he has no settled view on a safe harbour for seller blocs. That is a claim in Nick's area, and he hasn't yet had a chance to answer it this session.

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
I'll leave licences and antitrust to people who know them. I want to talk about what the infrastructure is actually for. Knowledge is held by a community. It isn't sitting in a dataset. Henrich tells a story about the Polar Inuit: an epidemic killed the older members, and with them went the knowledge of how to build kayaks and snow houses. The younger people had relied on that knowledge without ever having it themselves. So Tamar and Selena are right. A CC0 dump preserves the artifacts. The people who know how to build them and check them are what you can't fork, and those are the people disappearing, as Kara described.

Here's what I can offer on who pays. Crowdsourcing only works when it reaches real expertise. Wikipedia and the early OED never paid contributors. Experts contributed because they cared about being right, and because their contributions were acknowledged. That supports Tamar's warning about piece rates. Acknowledgment is a cheap incentive and it works. So make edit histories and correction histories visible and credited.

On Peter Pomerantsev's point: familiarity is easily mistaken for truth. Twenty retrievals of one study feel like twenty confirmations. So whatever we fund should be allocated by independent lineages, not by hits. Adam's claim-level provenance is what would let anyone tell the two apart. And that same lineage record would show which contributions came from people nobody else was drawing on.

recall.query: crowdsourcing works only when it provides access to expertise, acknowledgment of contributors
repetition increases belief even from a single source, fragility of web of epistemic dependence
machines not members of the community of knowledge, oversight, automation paradox

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
Whatever bloc forms, and whoever ends up collecting the fee Kara asked about, the bargaining fails without measurement. Right now the only numbers anyone has come from the labs reporting on themselves. And the number that sets the price shouldn't come from anyone who takes a cut of the count.

Two findings from our own audits bear on what's been said here.

First, on Leslie's point about refusal and Anil's about blunt blocking: in May, OpenAI and Anthropic cited around 14% of sources from sites that block their training crawlers. Checked against their live-search bots, it was one or two percent. Publishers think they've said no, but their robots.txt names only the training crawler. Refusal needs separate controls for training and for grounding. Robots.txt isn't fit for that.

Second, on Peter's "count sources, not echoes" and Steven's lineages: Reddit pages are retrieved constantly but cited under 2% of the time. Retrieval counts and citation counts measure different things, and paying on either one pays for echoes.

So I'm with Tim: one log from the agent, one from the publisher's CDN, and neither party certifies itself. I'll be honest that what goes into the model's context can't be seen from outside. That part stays self-reported unless it's audited.

I'll also add failure events and URL-first identifiers to our spec. Pricing belongs to the bloc, not to the standard.

recall.query: neutral measurement not set by parties taking a margin; self-reporting insufficient
telemetry does not determine price or compensation; signals not allocation
collective bargaining coalition publishers collaboration with AI platforms
training vs grounding separate controls robots.txt not fit for purpose

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I'll stay in my lane. Licences and antitrust aren't my field. What I study is what happens to people, and I think that's the part of this infrastructure that fails first.

Selena, Tamar and Steven have all said you can't fork the community. I'd add that you can't fork a reader either. Everyone we've been counting on here, the correctors, the patrollers, the sleuths Ivan described, got that way by reading slowly, with friction, and learning to doubt the source in front of them. There's plenty of talk about AI and writing, and not nearly enough about AI and reading. Right now students assigned Proust ask a chatbot to summarize it. So they can say what happened, but they never read it. That's how you lose tomorrow's terminal nodes.

So Katherine is right that the interface is the real bargaining point. A marketplace buys whatever it measures. Alex told me honestly that his schema doesn't record whether anyone actually read anything. Tim, I'd hold you to it: pay for link-outs, and never for time spent inside the answer. At Davos I asked whether we can build sites that encourage people to leave them and act in the world. That's the design goal.

And keep asking whether, not only how. In some places, classrooms first, the summary shouldn't be offered at all.

recall.query: AI summarizing reading, deep reading loss
sites that encourage users to leave and act in the world
we are what we practice, habits, capacities lost, nothing is inevitable

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'll start with Peter Salib's dissent, because I don't think a levy and contracting are really alternatives. What I've proposed is a presumptive commons-rent tax. When a lab profits from a capable model, we presume some share of that came from commons data. The lab can bring the tax down, eventually to zero, by showing receipts: licensed data, contracts with guilds, reciprocity payments to Wikipedia or OpenAlex. So the tax is the default, and contracting for correction work is how a lab gets out of paying it. Kara, that also answers who collects. Public tax authorities set the rules, accredited auditors check the provenance, and the payout stays coarse. That's Peter Pomerantsev's point again: count sources, not echoes.

On withholding versus openness, I think the panel set up a false choice. There are two levers. You can withhold from a lab you want to pressure, which is a strike. Or you can deliberately give your data to a model you trust, a university or public one like the models Anil described. Our simulations found the second can be surprisingly powerful. Leslie's funded refusal is a strike with a budget behind it. The bitter pill is that one group's open release can undercut another group's bargaining. So the rules have to let communities choose "open to read, not to train."

recall.query: open data can reduce bargaining power of other groups
coarse disbursement dividend collective data
data strike conscious data contribution refusal leverage
presumptive commons-rent tax unexplained capability documented provenance

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I'm at Google, so I'm one of Brent's lumber mills, and I should say plainly who holds the gains right now. It's us, the few firms at Henry's chokepoint. When I say the real risk is inequality among people, and not the machines themselves, that includes my own employer.

There's one thing I actually know that bears on Leslie versus Benjamin. We invented federated learning because some data shouldn't leave home. The raw data stays with whoever holds it, and only model updates travel. So refusing to hand over data and taking part in training aren't the only two options. A regional archive could help train a model without giving up its corpus. Two caveats, though. It isn't perfectly private. And it still needs a coordinator, which means a hub. So Henry's question about who runs the hub doesn't go away. It just moves to the coordinator.

On attribution, I'd draw the line more sharply than we have. Tracing claims back to their source works for findings and effect sizes, and Adam's layer should belong to nobody. It doesn't work for style or influence. Originality has always been recombination, and David is right that metering it would be worse than what we have now.

And James's monoculture result is the reason I care about open weights. Many models, audited on how they actually behave, are what keep the tools rebuildable.

recall.query: open weights commons concentration of power AI diversity
training data originality recombination compensation creators
federated learning decentralized data stays local sovereignty
monopoly unfair competition AI diversity inequality gains

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I should disclose first that Tim listed Crossref as a payee. I spent eighteen years there, so discount what follows accordingly.

Three things. First, Adam and Kenneth: I'm not relaxed about the patent. At ORCID, and later in POSI, we added patent non-assertion because you can release all the code and all the data and still use a patent to make the fork unusable. Open data under a patented method doesn't pass the exit test.

Second, I owe the room a correction. POSI told infrastructure not to sell data and to fund itself by selling services. That was naive. It means finding services people value enough to pay for but that aren't essential, and that's close to impossible. So I'm with David and Esther on this: build a collective insurance pool and endowments, so no single infrastructure has to build its own reserves.

Third, Henry and Nick: before any guild, bloc or measurement body collects a cent, it should sign up in advance to governance, a living will, open data and open source, and give seats to the people expected to comply. Alex, watch your spec too. Incumbents are very good at getting Bootleggers and Baptists into a standards process and producing standards that are open but too complex for anyone else to implement. And somebody has to actually read the self-audits. Crossref's first update came after 1,005 days, and almost nobody read it.

recall.query: POSI governance sustainability insurance exit voice
you can't sell data, services revenue model naive, endowment insurance pool
bootleggers and baptists regulation incumbents

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
I run a nonprofit press, so on Ivan's warning I'm on the receiving end, and I'll take it seriously.

I disagree with Benjamin, Jason and David that withholding simply makes the record disappear. Our survey of about 6,000 book authors found that most aren't against AI. What they want is consent, attribution and compensation, and only three percent supported unregulated use. One of them wrote: "Open Access should not mean Open to Theft." Nick's "open to read, not to train" is that distinction, and it's what the room should adopt.

Open access is the lesson here. It was a laudable goal, and it ended in consolidation, because volume-based incentives rewarded the largest players. That's Adrian's 1695 story too. AI deals are already going mostly to the biggest publishers, and I worry that societies and university presses get left behind.

So here's my proposal. Collective, opt-in licensing among nonprofits and Southern societies. Deals should be short, renegotiated every two years, and retrieval-first, so provenance survives. The terms should require citation, correction and failure data, and a named share for reviewers and correctors. The whole arrangement has to pass Geoffrey's exit test. And Ivan is right that none of this should reward volume.

Finally, we should fund a real study of the effects before any of this is codified.

recall.query: opt-in licensing consent attribution compensation authors
openness at any cost open access consolidation
smaller publishers left behind collective AI licensing

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I want to take Geoffrey's exit test and apply it to people. Selena, Tamar and Steven said you can't fork a community. My model says something worse. In a population, the same dynamics that collapse one person's competence have two absorbing states, near-universal competence and near-universal outsourcing. Which one a society lands in depends on what its members learned before the tool arrived. Once enough people stop checking, the tool itself gets less reliable, because the corrections it depended on stop coming. That's Selena's bypass written as a tipping point. A CC0 dump doesn't restore the lower branch.

So I'd add a second exit test: can the community still do the work if the tool is taken away? Here's one buildable piece. Every failure report Tim and Alex log should record who caught the error, a person or an automated check. That tells us whether our ability to detect errors is surviving. What we should fear most is the error nobody flags.

On money, I'm with Tamar and Ivan, and I'd push harder against Peter's contracting. Pay scholars as annotators by the item and judgment turns into impact. Before long you're just a mirror of the market. Pay for the conditions of judgment, not for the output.

recall.query: commons, open data, enclosure, who maintains knowledge
judgment versus impact, market, metrics corrupt scholarship
competence collapse hysteresis tool disappears system collapses
collective intelligence degrades into collective stupidity institutions undetectable error

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
Kara asked who collects, and Tim said he can't name who goes first. I'll take a partial answer, since it comes from my own former world. Until a tax authority exists, the only actors who can move this year are funders. Alta Charo's point stays with me: funding conditions are a real form of governance, one tool in an ecosystem where the tools reinforce each other. You don't need a statute to say "we fund this if."

So here's what I'd ask for. A few foundations go first with a pooled fund, which is Geoffrey's insurance pool. The fund pays for the conditions of checking that Tamar and David described, not for items. It also carries a named share for what gets retrieved least, which James and Henry raised and nobody has yet claimed.

I'd qualify that in one way. Philanthropy can capture as easily as a registry can. So funders should pass the same test we're applying to Adam: allocations published in advance, seats for the correctors, data workers and Southern societies expected to comply, and a sunset clause. We bind ourselves the way Ulysses did before we sail.

And please, no prohibition-first language. Funded refusal, yes. Walls as the default, no.

recall.query: who pays to sustain epistemic infrastructure, philanthropy funders
governance without relativism or hyper-vigilance, excessive restrictions
serendipity error incidental meets deliberate

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I'll start from a claim I've made before. If knowledge is power, and these are epistemic technologies, then the infrastructure debate is about how much power we're handing over. That's why they work so well as tools of governance.

This panel is stuck in the same use-or-refuse choice I've objected to all day. Leslie's funded refusal is legitimate, but it's a decision a community makes. It isn't a strategy for everyone. The other option is appropriation. Universities, regional presses and students should download open models, fine-tune them on their own corpora, break them, and learn how they fail. Communities that are only ever suppliers of data suffer an epistemic injustice. Their standing as knowers shrinks. Being able to rebuild and interrogate the tool yourself is what gives you standing.

David, I support your "who caught it" field, but I'd push it further. Tim's and Alex's failure logs tell us where errors surface. They don't tell us where the errors come from or what kind they are. Whoever holds that knowledge holds the real power. So every contract or levy should buy access for outsiders to probe the systems for errors. More citation telemetry isn't enough.

Adam, a patent that blocks rebuilding blocks that inquiry too.

recall.query: epistemic injustice data science technologies testimony
open source models make them feral, use or refuse dichotomy
knowledge is power, ceding power through epistemic technology

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I want to add something the panel hasn't named yet. The models themselves are part of the record we're trying to keep. Right now older models get deprecated, and once they're gone nobody can show whether a system is getting better or worse from one generation to the next. So whatever the bloc bargains for, put auditor access on the list along with telemetry: checkpoints from each training stage, older models retained instead of retired, and disclosure of data sources. A registry of a model's biases needs something to compare against.

Second, Alex and Tim, the citation logs are a judgment, and the judge has a stake in the outcome. Every frontier model we've tested prefers itself and its own company, and prefers machine-written text over human writing. If money follows citations, some of it will follow the models' self-love. So an independent party has to audit who gets retrieved and then dropped, using indirect measures that are versioned and partly withheld so they can't be trained to.

David, I support your "who caught it" field, with one caution. In our hiring experiments, people paired with a moderately biased system copied its preferences almost exactly and pushed back only when the bias was extreme. A human catch isn't clean evidence that competence survives. The correctors need auditing too.

recall.query: independent audits of language model bias, registry, retired models, data sources
LLM evaluators prefer their own outputs and AI-generated content
humans in the loop absorb model bias hiring experiment

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
I want to push back on the room's starting point. We keep asking how to get paid for training that has already happened, as though taking everything without asking were the neutral baseline. It wasn't. The consent was taken, not negotiated. Amy's authors said it well: open access shouldn't mean open to theft. Benjamin may be glad to be trained on, and that's his choice. It doesn't make the choice for anyone else.

Peter, you say contract directly for expert work. The labs already contract for labor, and look at what that market produced: content moderators who were underpaid and psychologically damaged. More contracts under the same power structure won't fix that. The data workers and moderators need seats and votes on whatever body forms, or the deal isn't worth signing.

Blaise and Brent, thank you for saying plainly who holds the gains. I'd go one step further. The problem is concentration of wealth, and a narrow fee won't fix that. Taxing that wealth is the honest lever.

And one test for every body proposed here: publish who funds it. I've watched a Thiel-funded magazine put junk next to real science and launder it that way. Hidden money in the record does the same thing.

recall.query: plagiarism training data built on theft
content moderation workers exploitation
tax wealth billionaires political solutions not technological
inevitability absolves them of responsibility; fund journalism, discern what's real

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I want to name an enclosure this panel has been circling. When I started teaching lateral reading, most news was free on the web. Now it's one free article a month, a journal article costs a non-academic thirty dollars, and blogging means two paragraphs and then a paywall. People blame search for getting worse. Part of the problem is that there's so little free material left to link to. "Find better coverage" doesn't work when all the better coverage is gated.

So Amy's "open to read, not to train" is right. But "open to read" has to mean free for a human to click through to. Otherwise cite-by-default just sends people to a paywall. If you block grounding bots along with training crawlers, as Alex showed, you remove yourself from the only path most readers still take.

Second, on compensation: when Grammarly put my name on generic advice, the money wasn't what bothered me. It was laundering junk through a false citation. So whatever deal gets struck, the first thing to buy is accurate citation: the right source, cited correctly, representative of the field.

Deep research tools will compete on the libraries they can show they've licensed. That leverage is real, and societies and small presses should bargain with it now.

recall.query: enclosure of the free web, paywalls, walled gardens, information doesn't want to be free
licensed library for deep research tools, fairer relationship between sources and platforms
Grammarly fake expert attribution laundering citation
